briefOverview: A closing apocalypse that promises deliverance and resurrection at the end-time while giving cryptic chronological markers to be sealed until the end.
summary: Michael, the great prince, will arise at an unprecedented time of trouble to protect Daniel’s people and secure the deliverance of those whose names are written in the book. The chapter affirms a resurrection in which some awake to everlasting life and others to shame, and praises the wise who bring others to righteousness. Daniel is instructed to seal the words until the time of the end; the vision notes increased movement and knowledge in that period. A figure asks how long the wonders will last and is answered with the period 'a time, times, and an half' and statements about the scattering of the holy people. The text then gives precise day-numbers—1,290 and 1,335 days—and blesses the one who waits to reach the latter date. The book closes with an exhortation that Daniel rest until he is raised to his allotted place at the end of days.
externalContext: Most scholars place the final layers of Daniel in the Hellenistic period (2nd century BCE), during the crisis under Seleucid ruler Antiochus IV Epiphanes; this context helps explain the text’s focus on an 'abomination that maketh desolate' and on persecution of the cult. Jewish apocalyptic literature of this era commonly uses symbolic time periods (e.g., 3.5 years = 'time, times, and a half') and angelic mediators like Michael to express hope for divine vindication. The explicit assertion of a resurrection (v.2) is one of the clearest early Jewish statements of afterlife vindication and became influential in later Jewish and Christian thinking.
externalReferences: The figure Michael is also prominent in Daniel 10 (see Daniel 10:13,21), where he assists the heavenly messenger, and Daniel 8:14 and 8:26 provide earlier calendrical and sealing motifs that this chapter echoes. The phrase 'abomination that maketh desolate' appears elsewhere in Daniel (9:27; 11:31) and is explicitly cited in the New Testament (Matthew 24:15) as a marker for end-time warning. The symbolic period 'a time, times, and an half' is common in apocalyptic texts and is often read alongside other Daniel time periods (e.g., the 1,290 and 1,335 days here and the 2,300 evenings and mornings in Daniel 8:14) when interpreters attempt chronological correlations.
practicalQuestions: How does the promise of resurrection and final vindication shape personal and communal ethics in times of suffering?
What does it mean today to be among those 'wise' who 'turn many to righteousness' and how can communities cultivate that wisdom?
How should modern readers approach sealed or symbolic prophetic language—what posture of humility and study is appropriate?
When a text gives precise but obscure timetables, how ought believers balance the desire for certainty with the possibility of symbolic time-frames?
uncertainAreas: The precise meaning and chronological application of the time periods (e.g., 'time, times, and an half,' 1,290 and 1,335 days) is debated—whether they are literal days, symbolic periods, or tied to specific historical events (such as Antiochus IV's persecutions) is uncertain. The identity and scope of 'the wicked' versus 'the wise' and the mechanics of the 'book' that records the saved are not fully explained in the text and remain open to interpretation.
